support.quote:
This relationship is compared to the results from material flammability 
tests in a highspeed blow-off facility at the NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) (1-g) and 
the Glenn Research Center (GRC) Zero Gravity Facility partial gravity centrifuge.

Experimental Method 
The goal was to measure the change in the extinction limit between 1-g testing and lunar-g testing in the centrifuge.

Consequently a 5 second extinction criterion test program was developed to determine the change in the 
extinction limit in 1-g and lunar-g and apply this offset to NASA Test 1 flammability limits for lunar material 
certification.

6 
International Conference on Environmental Systems 
 
 
the planned NASA lunar habitat pressure of 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia) for several materials where the higher speed blow-off 
behavior in 1-g could be compared to the flame extinguishment in lunar-gravity buoyant flow.

This required a test 
program that included work at the NASA White Sands Test Facility (WSTF) for the 1-g buoyant flow testing and the 
NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) Zero-Gravity Research Facility (ZGRF) for a quiescent lunar gravity 
environment.

During the ignition interval, the drop 
rig is hanging at the top of the tower and is spinning to produce a 1/6 g radial acceleration in addition to the 1-g vertical 
force.

To estimate the change in the flammability limit at 1-g  compared to lunar-g, the 
extrapolated value from the WSTF testing can be compared to the extrapolated value at lunar g.

The 1-g buoyant velocity was estimated by Takahashi16 to be 35 cm/s, 
but the lunar gravity velocity is not known.

Given this uncertainty, 35 cm/s could be considered to be a 
conservatively high estimate of the buoyant 1-g velocity.

Extrapolating the worst-case 95% confidence interval slope 
from the data for each material (Table 2) from the presumed 1-g buoyant velocity of 35 cm/s to zero would give a 
conservative 1-g to lunar-g flammability delta that could be applied to other test methods.

Conclusion 
Comparative testing in 1-g under forced flow and buoyant flow at lunar-g conditions has demonstrated that for 
some materials, there is a clear increased flammability at lunar gravity conditions.

Other, higher temperature materials 
may show decreased flammability at lunar conditions than would be predicted from 1-g testing.
